title: Lesson 58: Local Models: Running Open Weights, Quantization, and Hardware
description: Running open-weight models on hardware you control: what quantization does to memory, the 0.6 GB per billion parameters rule of thumb, the formats (GGUF, GPTQ, AWQ) and engines (llama.cpp, Ollama, vLLM, MLX), and what actually bounds single-stream speed.

questions.question: Per the lesson, why does quantization usually come before any other decision when you are choosing a model for a local machine?
options: It has no real effect, because every model loads at its full precision no matter how it is stored
It only changes the training cost, not the memory needed to run the model
It stores weights in fewer bits, shrinking a model's memory footprint by about four times at 4-bit versus 16-bit, which is what decides whether the weights fit in VRAM or unified memory at all
It only applies to GGUF files and never to the engines that actually run the model
questions.explanation: Quantization stores each weight in fewer bits, so a 7B model drops from roughly 14 GB of fp16 weights to roughly 4 GB at 4-bit. That is the lever that lets a small GPU or a laptop hold a model that otherwise would never fit.

questions.question: Using the lesson's rule of thumb, about how much memory should an 11-billion-parameter model's weights need at 4-bit quantization?
options: About 2 GB, because parameter count is unrelated to memory
About 6.6 GB, from budgeting roughly 0.6 GB per billion parameters
About 22 GB, because each parameter always needs two bytes regardless of how it is stored
Exactly 11 GB, because one billion parameters equals one gigabyte
questions.explanation: The lesson's rule of thumb is roughly 0.6 GB of memory per billion parameters at 4-bit. For 11 billion parameters that is about 6.6 GB of weights, before adding context-window and runtime headroom.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what mainly sets the single-stream speed of a locally running model for one user?
options: How fast memory can move the model's weights into the compute units, roughly tokens per second equals memory bandwidth divided by bytes of model
The exact spelling of the prompt, because tokenization dominates all latency
The number of concurrent users, because one user always runs at the same speed no matter the hardware
The network round trip to the model provider, since local models still depend on a hosted API
questions.explanation: For one user, inference is bounded by how quickly the machine can stream weights from memory into the compute units. A smaller quantized model moves fewer bytes per token, which is why it feels faster on the same hardware.
